https://www.dw.com/en/how-germany-suppor.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IpgO Commemorations for the victims of the Berlin Pride attack started arriving mere hours after the attack Image: IMAGO/Wolfgang Maria Weber Advertisement On the evening of July 25, according to German authorities, Abdul Ballout, drove a white van into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate, where thousands were celebrating Berlin Pride. He then got out of the vehicle and began attacking people at random with a large knife. He killed a 65-year-old woman from Poland and injured her daughter, along with 30 other people, some of them seriously. Many details have emerged about Ballout, his links to extremists, his criminal record and his family. A day after the incident, he was shot dead by police officers while trying to flee during an arrest attempt. The identities of the victims, and how they are coping after the attack on the event celebrating LGBTQ+ rights , are not publicly known. Still, many are likely to live with its consequences for months, if not years, to come. The only details disclosed by Berlin's governing mayor concern the age and nationality of the woman who was killed. Otherwise, Germany's strict data protection laws protect victims' privacy. Victims can approach the media themselves at any time if they choose to make their stories public, Roland Weber, the German federal government's commissioner for victims of terrorism and extremist violence , told DW. Calls for political consequences after Berlin Pride attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Support for the victims In Germany , people affected by such attacks are often reluctant to come forward publicly or identify themselves as victims, said Julia Kühne. She should know: Kühne is the spokesperson for the Association for Victims of Terrorism ( VoT Germany ), which is part of an international federation of terrorism victims. "The perpetrator needs to disappear from the media, now that he has been caught and killed. Those affected should naturally be brought much more to the forefront," said Kühne. How are those who were injured in the attack doing today? Weber has visited some of them in hospital. "What I saw there was distressing. But thanks to modern medicine, and because the doctors are optimistic, there is reason for hope that everyone will recover as fully as possible," he said. "In some cases, however, that remains uncertain. Only time will tell. Some of the injured have already been discharged from hospital and are now receiving outpatient treatment. Others will begin various forms of therapy and rehabilitation." How are the victims being supported? The Federal Commissioner for Victims and Weisser Ring , a victim support organization, arrange trauma treatment , provide immediate financial assistance, and advise victims on long-term care and victims' pensions. Weisser Ring is a volunteer-run organization that works closely with the police to provide advice and support to victims of crime in Germany. "In cases of terrorist attacks, there is also a special provision: victims can apply for hardship payments," said Weber. "These are funds made available by the Bundestag. Hardly anyone knows about them, and making people aware of them is part of our job. We provide guidance and help ensure that applications are submitted as quickly as possible." Germany reviews Berlin Pride attack security failures To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Weber is also responsible for supporting the relatives of the Polish woman who was killed and her daughter, who was injured in the attack. Nationality is not a factor in this regard. He assists victims with follow-up costs and compensation whenever an act of terrorism or extremist violence has been committed on German soil. Number of traumatized victims still unclear The victims of the attack are not only those who sustained physical injuries. According to VoT Germany's Kühne, even people who witnessed the attack from several hundred meters away may be considered victims. "There are people who do not develop problems until years later," she told DW. "They may suddenly begin to suffer from sleep disturbances, experience nightmares, develop panic attacks or struggle with social phobia. In some cases, these symptoms do not emerge until years afterward because those affected were initially either still in shock or had returned to their everyday lives and were therefore able, at least to some extent, to suppress what they had experienced." Kühne also noted that survivors of previous terrorist attacks may be retraumatized by media coverage of the current attack in Berlin and find themselves in need of support once again. She knows this from personal experience: she herself survived the 2016 attack on Berlin's Christmas market, which ultimately claimed 13 lives and left more than 70 injured. In the shadow of RAF terror: The children left behind To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Victim support: Problems in practice Weisser Ring, which supports victims of crime across Germany, believes adequate compensation schemes and pension entitlements for victims of terrorism are now in place. However, not everything runs smoothly in practice, said Rolf Schmachtenberg, the organization's state chairman in Berlin. "In cases where people have suffered permanent harm, the assessment procedures are often quite lengthy," he said. "We also continue to encounter administrative bottlenecks, with some authorities still relying on paper files and fax communications. They then have to wait for information from other agencies, which can significantly delay the application process. In my view, the main problem is one of implementation." Over the past decade, Germany has experienced 13 terrorist attacks motivated by Islamist or political extremist ideologies, leaving 39 people dead and 475 injured. The support provided by the federal government's commissioner for victims has no time limit. Weber continues to assist people affected by attacks dating back to the 1980s. Commemoration continues of the nine people killed in 2020 in a racially motivated terrorist attack in the city of Hanau Image: Kadir Ilboga/Anadolu/picture alliance Victims seek answers For many victims, coming to terms with the horror and suffering also means finding answers to the question of why the perpetrator acted and why they, in particular, were targeted, said Weber. In some court proceedings, perpetrators have remained silent. In the case of the Berlin Pride attack, however, the perpetrator was killed, meaning there will never be complete clarity about his motives. In Germany, investigations are discontinued once a suspect has died. No court will ever determine whether Abdul Ballout selected his victims for one particular reason or another. "As a result, some questions will remain unanswered," said Weber. "The search for answers is something most victims have in common, but it cannot always lead to certainty." This article was originally written in German. Accident investigations typically yield rare, if not unprecedented, combinations of technical failure and human error. Photograph: Guardia Civil/AFP/Getty Images Spain Explainer How did the Spain train crash happen and what will investigators be asking? Audio file appears to point finger at control centre, but there are questions around signalling and technical issues Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.39 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 69 people died when a high-speed train from Madrid to Seville hit another train on the same track from behind near Toledo on Wednesday morning. Both trains had been brought to a halt earlier when the signalling system failed. The driver of the state-owned Spanish train, a Renfe AVE service, was told by controllers to restart the journey, but crashed into the train in front, run by the private operator Iryo. The front carriages of the AVE train and rear of the Iryo train were destroyed and others derailed. How could this happen? The nature of this disaster, as well as its human toll, seems particularly shocking. There are multiple safeguards on high-speed lines, including different types of automatic train operation, which should ensure trains are never able to come close on the same track. The audio file released to Spanish media by the government appears to point the finger at the control centre, with a controller in Madrid telling the driver of the halted AVE train to proceed “ con marcha normal ” – under normal operations – rather than at low speed. The instruction was described by the transport minister, Óscar Puente, as an “inexplicable decision”. Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network Read more Has this happened before? Rear-end collisions are rare, as are any kind of crash between trains on international high-speed networks. The closest comparator occurred in China in 2011, when a high-speed train hit a stationary express in front of it in Wenzhou, killing 40 people. The rear-end collision between two East Midlands trains in Bedford this year was the first fatal crash of that kind in 40 years in the UK, and occurred on a stretch of railway without automatic train operation, after the driver apparently failed to slow despite the danger signal. What will investigators be asking? While the audio appears to indicate human error played a central role, there are other elements that remain unclear, such as what caused the initial failure of the signalling system. The German-designed train control system is being phased out and the CEO of Iryo recently told a senate inquiry that disconnection was a “frequent issue” on the line. Investigators will be looking at the sequence of events and technical issues that allowed the Renfe train to proceed but the Iryo train to stay put. ‘People were thrown in the air’: passenger recounts moment train crashed in Spain – video Signallers, or track controllers, are increasingly based in remote computer centres but are acutely aware of the risk and responsibility their job entails. Any investigation will want to establish what circumstances or pressures could have led to that instruction. In all modern hi-tech transport, whether air or rail, known safety risks are eradicated as far as possible. Accident investigations typically yield rare, if not unprecedented, combinations of technical failure and human error. ‘It all happened in a split second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain Read more What does it mean for Spain? The Spanish government will want to demonstrate that this latest disaster is completely unconnected to the head-on crash between two trains that occurred on the same line in Adamuz in January after one derailed, apparently due to a small section of faulty or missing rail. Train drivers were due to strike, even before this week’s crash, in protest against under-investment in the railway and its people, which unions say is directly connected to safety. The success of Spain’s high-speed railway, linking Madrid to Seville and Barcelona, was the envy of British rail planners. It was modern and had cut journeys from the capital to Andalusia to two and a half hours; a car takes twice that, and the public transport alternative of the coach, three times as long. Good public transportation links bring jobs and growth; losing them could mean the opposite. Are Europe’s railways safe? The long-term trend since 2010 has been fewer fatalities of any sort on the railway. Most years, in most countries, no passenger is killed in any type of train crash, a world away from the death toll on the roads. However, worries about under-investment in the railways, particularly after costs and subsidy soared as fare revenue dried up in the pandemic, are not unique to Spain.
